questions.q: What question does Azure RBAC actually answer, as distinct from Azure Policy?
options: Can this principal attempt this action at all, evaluated at authorization time before anything happens
Is this resource's current configuration compliant with an organizational standard
Does this resource have a related resource, like a diagnostic setting, attached to it
Should this resource's tags be automatically rewritten at write time
questions.explain: RBAC is evaluated by Azure Resource Manager at authorization time and governs whether a principal can attempt an action at all — the other options describe things Azure Policy evaluates.

questions.q: In an RBAC role definition, what is the purpose of the `NotActions` field?
options: It lists data-plane operations the role can never perform under any circumstances
It carves exclusions out of a broader `Actions` wildcard, which is how roles like Contributor are built from `*` minus certain permissions
It defines which Azure Policy effects the role is allowed to trigger
It specifies the resource group the role definition is stored in
questions.explain: NotActions subtracts specific operations from a wildcard Actions grant — Contributor, for example, is effectively "*" minus the ability to grant access to others.

questions.q: Which Azure Policy effect actively remediates a non-compliant setup by deploying a missing related resource?
options: Audit
AuditIfNotExists
DeployIfNotExists
Deny
questions.explain: DeployIfNotExists goes beyond flagging non-compliance — it deploys the missing related resource itself, using a managed identity with its own scoped RBAC permissions.

questions.q: Why can an Azure Owner still be blocked from creating a storage account with public blob access enabled, even though RBAC grants Owners unrestricted Actions?
options: Because Owner is actually a read-only role for storage accounts specifically
Because Azure Policy requires its own separate RBAC role assignment before it can evaluate anything
Because DataActions for storage accounts are always denied by default regardless of role
Because a Deny-effect policy evaluates the resource's own configuration directly, independent of who the caller is or what RBAC permits them to attempt
questions.explain: RBAC authorizes the attempt based on identity; Policy separately evaluates the resulting resource's configuration and can deny it regardless of the caller's role.

questions.q: A subscription requires that only the platform team can create storage accounts, AND that every storage account must have public blob access disabled. Why does this require both RBAC and Policy rather than either alone?
options: Because Azure Policy cannot be assigned at the subscription scope
Because RBAC restricts who can attempt the creation, but has no concept of a storage account's public-access property, which only Policy evaluates
Because RBAC roles expire automatically after 90 days and must be paired with Policy to persist
Because Azure Policy effects always override RBAC role assignments entirely
questions.explain: RBAC alone would stop the wrong people from creating storage accounts but miss a misconfiguration by the right people; Policy alone would catch the misconfiguration but not restrict who can attempt creation.
